[ saṃ + kappa + a.]  CL=7 (1) (The object or basis) that is intended and longed. (Pu) (2) Types of Thoughts or Intentions: (A) A good thought or intention. (B) A wrong or unwholesome thought or intention. (C) Both good and bad thoughts or intentions. (D) A thought related to sensual pleasure (kāma). (E) A thought related to kāma, byāpāda (ill-will), vihaṃsā (cruelty), or diṭṭhi (wrong view). (3) Mental Processes or Actions: (A) (A) Intending or contemplating.
(B) Well-formed or wholesome thinking (linked to vitakka cetasika, the mental factor of applied thought). (4) Greed or craving (lobha) that arises from contemplating forms, signs, or characteristics (nimitta and anubyañjana). (5) A thought or intention directed towards a sense object or mind object. (6) Wishing or praying for one’s desires to be fulfilled. (7) Deliberate intention motivated by goodwill or positive volition. (8) (A) Desire or craving. (B) The desire of the heart or mind (deeper emotional longing). (9) (A) Judging, deciding, or forming a conclusion. (B) Establishing the three factors: perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), and applied thought (vitakka). (10) Saṅkappavagga (Section on Thought): Refers to the discourse or teachings related to thoughts or intentions (e.g., as found in the Dhammapada).

saṅkhata:
[ saṃ + kara + ta.]  CL=7 (1) The volitional transformation dhamma, which is the conditioned dhamma arranged and reformed by causes: (A) The five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā). (B) The aggregate of mental activity (saṅkhārakkhandha). (C) Aggregates (khandhā), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). (D) The three-tiered dhamma (tebhūmaka dhamma). (E) The three noble truths: dukkha (suffering), samudaya (origin), and magga (path). (F) The characteristics of transformation (saṅkhāra sabhāva). (G) The physical body (khandhakāya). (H) Dependent origination dhamma (paṭiccasamuppāda dhamma). (I) Liking and disliking (sāratta and nīratta). (J) The set of dhammas beginning with the eye and ending with dependent origination. (K) Views and clinging to views (diṭṭhi and diṭṭhupādāna). (L) Pride or conceit (māna). (M) The immaterial absorptions (arūpajhāna). (N) All perceptions (saññā). (O) The jhāna without perception (asaññā jhāna). (P) The dimension of neither perception nor non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana jhāna). (Q) The doctrine of annihilation (ucchedavāda). (R) The first jhāna with delight (sappītika jhāna). (S) The peace and tranquility of the third jhāna. (T) Neutral feeling (upekkhā vedanā) associated with the fourth jhāna. (U) Light, brightness, or radiance (āloka). (2) Rice porridge cooked with milk. (3) The commentary that should be written or composed. (4) That which should be adorned or decorated. (5) The noble path (ariyamagga) that should be practiced in various ways. (6) saṅkhatalakkhaṇasutta, aṅguttara nikāya 3.47 (AN3.47). (7) That which is arranged and reformed through the combination of causes. (8) Arranging or reforming the meaning (attha).

In detail: It encompasses all sentient beings who exist due to causes and conditions, explained through the lens of puggaladhiṭṭhāna desanā (teaching based on the concept of beings). Their existence fundamentally depends on causes, making them undeniably part of the conditioned world (saṅkhāradhamma).
